blocks.content: When your browser opens a website, data travels from your application, down through your operating system, over a wire, across routers, and back up through a server's own stack, all within milliseconds. The OSI model gives every step of that journey a name and a clear responsibility.

OSI stands for Open Systems Interconnection. It splits network communication into seven layers, each one solving exactly one problem and handing its result to the next. Knowing which layer a problem actually lives in tells you precisely where to look when something breaks, which is why this model, more than thirty years old, is still the first thing engineers reach for when diagnosing a real outage.
1. The Seven Layers, Top to Bottom
blocks.text: 1. The Seven Layers, Top to Bottom

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024989-52527222.png
blocks.alt: Data flows down through all seven layers on the sender's side, and back up through all seven on the receiver's side

blocks.content: Sending data flows down through layers seven to one, with each layer adding its own header along the way. At the physical wire, only raw bits travel between machines. On arrival, the receiving side flows back up through layers one to seven, with each layer stripping off exactly the header the matching layer on the sender added.

blocks.title: Why Engineers Still Use This
blocks.content: When someone says this is a layer 3 issue, every other engineer instantly knows they mean IP routing, not an application bug. That shared vocabulary is the entire value of the OSI model, it is a diagnostic map, not a literal blueprint of how software is actually built today.
2. Layer 7: Application
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272973494-281919595.png
blocks.alt: The application layer is the one your own code directly interacts with

blocks.content: This is the layer your code touches directly. It defines how applications talk to each other, what a request looks like, what a response looks like, and how errors get reported. Every API you have ever called or designed lives here.
In high level design terms, choosing REST versus gRPC, designing a request contract, or deciding where a CDN sits in front of your API, all of that is layer 7 work.
3. Layer 6: Presentation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025327-923234595.png
blocks.alt: The presentation layer transforms application data into network ready bytes through encryption, compression, and encoding

blocks.content: This layer acts as the translator between application data and network ready bytes. Three transformations happen here. Encryption turns readable plaintext into secure ciphertext, using TLS, so nothing readable travels across the wire. Compression shrinks the payload, turning a large JSON body into a smaller gzip version to save bandwidth. Encoding changes the format entirely, converting an image into Base64 or raw bytes into UTF-8 text so it can travel safely.

In practice, most modern protocols fold this layer directly into layer 7. TLS is technically layer 6, but it is handled as part of HTTPS: your browser's HTTP request is built first, then TLS encrypts it before it ever leaves your machine, and on arrival the server decrypts it before handing the original, clean HTTP request back up to its own application layer.
4. Layer 5: Session
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272977183-454305782.png
blocks.alt: A session opens, stays active while data flows, and either closes cleanly or briefly resumes after an interruption

blocks.content: This layer manages the lifecycle of a connection between two applications, opening it, keeping it alive, and cleanly closing it. It also handles checkpointing, if a long transfer drops partway through, session management can pick back up rather than starting over from nothing.

In modern systems, layers 5 and 6 are rarely built as genuinely distinct pieces of software. HTTP keep alive, WebSocket connections, and gRPC streams all implement session concepts directly inside the application layer itself, rather than as a separate stack layer.

blocks.title: A Familiar Example
blocks.content: A two hour video call stays connected even when your WiFi briefly drops for a couple of seconds. The session layer's concept is exactly what keeps the call alive instead of tearing it down and forcing you to rejoin.
5. Layer 4: Transport
Layer 3 gets a packet to the right machine. Layer 4 gets it to the right process running on that machine, using port numbers. Port 443 means HTTPS, port 5432 means PostgreSQL, and so on.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272979080-352954274.png
blocks.alt: The same machine can run many services at once, port numbers are what route an arriving packet to the correct process

blocks.content: The TCP Three Way Handshake
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272980769-118848942.png
blocks.alt: A TCP connection is established through exactly three messages before either side sends any real data

blocks.content: ["The client sends a SYN message to the server, along with an initial sequence number, signaling I want to connect","The server replies with a SYN ACK, acknowledging the client's request and providing its own sequence number in return","The client sends a final ACK, and both sides are now synchronized, the connection is established and data can flow reliably in both directions"]
items: The client sends a SYN message to the server, along with an initial sequence number, signaling I want to connect
The server replies with a SYN ACK, acknowledging the client's request and providing its own sequence number in return
The client sends a final ACK, and both sides are now synchronized, the connection is established and data can flow reliably in both directions

6. Layer 3: Network
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272982451-829485364.png
blocks.alt: A packet hops from router to router, each one reading the destination address and forwarding it one step closer

blocks.content: This layer is responsible for getting a packet from a source machine to a destination machine across multiple networks. Layer 2 can only deliver within one local network, layer 3 can route across the entire internet.

The key device here is the router. A router reads the destination IP address on every incoming packet, checks its own routing table, and forwards the packet one hop closer to its destination, repeating this handoff, router to router, until the packet finally arrives.
7. Layer 2: Data Link
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272984028-487544026.png
blocks.alt: An Ethernet frame carries a preamble, destination and source MAC addresses, the actual payload, and a trailing check sequence

blocks.content: This layer works within a single local network. It takes raw bits from layer 1 and organizes them into frames, structured units carrying addressing information, using MAC addresses, hardware addresses burned into every network card, to identify devices sharing that same local segment.

The key device here is the switch. A switch learns which MAC address sits on which port and forwards a frame only to that correct destination port, unlike a hub, which broadcasts every frame to every port regardless of who it is actually meant for.
8. Layer 1: Physical
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272985674-372912522.png
blocks.alt: At the very bottom of the stack, only raw bits travel, as electrical pulses, light, or radio waves, with no concept of meaning at all

blocks.content: This is the bottom of the stack, raw bits on a physical medium, electrical pulses over copper, light through fiber, radio waves for WiFi. This layer has no concept of addresses, structure, or meaning whatsoever, it just moves ones and zeros.

blocks.title: No Software Fix Applies Here
blocks.content: A broken cable, a failing network card, or a dead port are physical problems, and no amount of clever code above this layer changes that. Everything above layer 1 is irrelevant until layer 1 itself actually works.
9. Encapsulation: What Actually Travels Over the Wire
blocks.text: 9. Encapsulation: What Actually Travels Over the Wire

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024510-866971821.png
blocks.alt: Each layer wraps the data from the layer above with its own header on the way down, over the wire, and each layer strips its own header back off on the way up

blocks.content: When you make an HTTPS request, each layer wraps the data handed down from the layer above it with its own header. On arrival, the process reverses, each layer unwraps its own part and passes the remaining payload up to the layer above. Wrapping on the way down is called encapsulation, unwrapping on the way up is called decapsulation.

Starting from HTTP data at the application layer, TLS at the presentation layer encrypts it, TCP at the transport layer adds its header for ports and sequencing, IP at the network layer adds source and destination addresses, and Ethernet at the data link layer wraps the whole thing into a frame ready for the wire. On the receiving side, Ethernet strips its frame, IP processes the routing information, TCP confirms correct delivery, TLS decrypts, and the original HTTP request arrives at the application layer exactly as it was sent.

The example below makes this concrete: a small program that encapsulates a plain HTTP request through four layers of headers, then decapsulates it back to the original, unmodified request, printing exactly what gets stripped at each step.

codes.python:
def encapsulate(payload):
    # Each layer wraps the payload from the layer above with its own header, in
    # order: presentation (TLS), transport (TCP), network (IP), data link (Ethernet).
    presentation_layer = f"[TLS]{payload}"
    transport_layer = f"[TCP:port=443]{presentation_layer}"
    network_layer = f"[IP:dst=93.184.216.34]{transport_layer}"
    data_link_layer = f"[ETH:dstMac=AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF]{network_layer}"
    return data_link_layer


def strip_header(data, expected_tag):
    end = data.index("]")
    tag = data[1:end]
    if not tag.startswith(expected_tag):
        raise ValueError(f"Expected {expected_tag} header, found {tag}")
    return data[end + 1:]


def decapsulate(frame):
    # Each layer strips its own header in reverse order, from the wire back up to the application.
    after_ethernet = strip_header(frame, "ETH")
    print("After removing the Ethernet frame:", after_ethernet)
    after_ip = strip_header(after_ethernet, "IP")
    print("After removing the IP header:", after_ip)
    after_tcp = strip_header(after_ip, "TCP")
    print("After removing the TCP header:", after_tcp)
    after_tls = strip_header(after_tcp, "TLS")
    print("After removing the TLS wrapper:", after_tls)
    return after_tls


def main():
    http_request = "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1"

    on_the_wire = encapsulate(http_request)
    print("On the wire:", on_the_wire)

    recovered = decapsulate(on_the_wire)
    print("Recovered at the application layer:", recovered)
    print("Matches original:", recovered == http_request)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: 10. OSI vs TCP/IP: What Actually Runs the Internet
blocks.text: 10. OSI vs TCP/IP: What Actually Runs the Internet

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272988895-749417331.png
blocks.alt: The internet actually runs on the simpler, four layer TCP/IP model, which collapses several OSI layers together

blocks.content: The OSI model is primarily a learning and diagnostic tool. The internet itself actually runs on the TCP/IP model, a simplified four layer version. Layers five, six, and seven of OSI all collapse into a single Application layer in TCP/IP, and layers one and two collapse into a single Link layer.

OSI's real value is not that software is literally built this way, it is precision in conversation. When an engineer says layer 3 issue, everyone immediately understands IP routing, and layer 4 issue immediately means TCP or UDP ports. TCP/IP's single, broad Application layer is simply too coarse for that kind of precise diagnosis.
11. A Common Mistake: Misdiagnosing Which Layer Failed
blocks.text: 11. A Common Mistake: Misdiagnosing Which Layer Failed

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272990584-373278762.png
blocks.alt: Assuming an outage is a network problem when it is actually an application bug wastes real time chasing the wrong layer entirely

blocks.content: A genuinely common failure mode is treating every outage as a network problem by default. Users reporting the site is down often triggers a reflexive check of routers and load balancers, when the actual fault is a deployment bug at layer 7 that has nothing to do with the network at all. Time spent restarting healthy infrastructure is time not spent finding the real, much simpler fix.

blocks.title: Diagnose Layer by Layer, Not by Instinct
blocks.content: Start from layer 1 only if there is a genuine physical signal, otherwise start by confirming whether the application itself is behaving correctly before assuming the problem lives anywhere lower in the stack.
Key Takeaway

The OSI model splits network communication into seven layers, application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link, and physical, each one solving exactly one problem and handing its result to the next. Data is wrapped with a header on the way down through every layer and unwrapped in reverse on the way up, and while the real internet runs on the simpler, four layer TCP/IP model, OSI remains the shared vocabulary engineers use to say precisely where in the stack a problem actually lives.
